chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content:
Source: National Weather Service (NOAA), "Heat Safety Tips and Resources — During".
Retrieved 2026-08-05. US federal government work, public domain.
chunks.heading: Extreme Heat — Protective Actions

chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content:
- Drink plenty of water, non-alcoholic and decaffeinated fluids, even if you do not feel thirsty.
- Avoid salt tablets unless prescribed by a physician.
chunks.heading: Hydration

chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content:
- Reduce, eliminate or reschedule strenuous activities until the coolest time of the day.
- Limit children's outdoor play to the cooler times of day.
chunks.heading: Timing and activity

chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content: - Wear lightweight, loose fitting, light-coloured clothing to reflect heat and sunlight.
chunks.heading: Clothing

chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content:
- Use air conditioning, or spend time in air-conditioned public spaces such as malls and libraries.
- Use portable fans to exhaust hot air or draw in cooler air.
- Do not direct a portable fan toward yourself when the room temperature is above 90F (32C).
- Take a cool bath or shower.
chunks.heading: Staying cool and shelter

chunks.title: Heat Safety — Actions During Extreme Heat
chunks.content:
- Check on older, sick, or frail people who may need help responding to the heat.
- Never leave children or pets unattended in a vehicle, even briefly.
chunks.heading: People at higher risk

chunks.title: UV Index Scale and Protective Actions
chunks.content:
Source: United States Environmental Protection Agency, "UV Index Scale".
Retrieved 2026-08-05. US federal government work, public domain.
chunks.heading: UV Index Scale — Protective Actions by Category

chunks.title: UV Index Scale and Protective Actions
chunks.content: - No protection needed. You can safely stay outside using minimal sun protection.
chunks.heading: UV Index 1 to 2 — Low

chunks.title: UV Index Scale and Protective Actions
chunks.content:
- Protection needed. Seek shade during late morning through mid-afternoon.
- Apply broad-spectrum SPF-15 or higher sunscreen on exposed skin.
- Wear protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and sunglasses.
chunks.heading: UV Index 3 to 7 — Moderate to High

chunks.title: UV Index Scale and Protective Actions
chunks.content:
- Extra protection needed. Be careful outside, especially during late morning through mid-afternoon.
- When your shadow is shorter than you are, seek shade.
- Wear protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and sunglasses.
- Generously apply a minimum of SPF-15 broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed skin.
chunks.heading: UV Index 8 and above — Very High to Extreme

chunks.title: Wind Safety — Actions During High Wind
chunks.content:
Source: National Weather Service (NOAA), "Wind Safety — During".
Retrieved 2026-08-05. US federal government work, public domain.
chunks.heading: High Wind — Protective Actions

chunks.title: Wind Safety — Actions During High Wind
chunks.content:
- Immediately go inside a sturdy building; move to an interior room.
- If you are in a mobile home, move to a sturdy building before the winds pick up.
- Listen to local news or NOAA Weather Radio for updates.
chunks.heading: Indoors

chunks.title: Wind Safety — Actions During High Wind
chunks.content:
- Take shelter in your car if no sturdy building is nearby.
- Avoid trees, power lines, and the side of the road.
- Find a place that will block blowing or falling debris.
- Do not approach power lines lying on the ground; they may be live.
chunks.heading: Outdoors

chunks.title: Wind Safety — Actions During High Wind
chunks.content:
- Move your car to a location where it is less likely to be hit by falling trees or power lines.
- When driving near a building, hold the steering wheel with both hands and slow down.
- Keep a distance from high profile vehicles such as trucks and buses; strong gusts can flip them.
chunks.heading: Driving

chunks.title: Wind Safety — Actions During High Wind
chunks.content:
- Get indoors, close all windows and turn off air conditioning units.
- If driving, pull the vehicle off the pavement as far as possible, stop, and turn off the lights.
chunks.heading: Blowing dust

chunks.title: Flood Safety — Actions During Heavy Rain and Flooding
chunks.content:
Source: National Weather Service (NOAA), "Flood Safety — During".
Retrieved 2026-08-05. US federal government work, public domain.
chunks.heading: Heavy Rain and Flooding — Protective Actions

chunks.title: Flood Safety — Actions During Heavy Rain and Flooding
chunks.content:
- Listen to radio and television, including NOAA Weather Radio if possible.
- If you live in a flood prone area or are camping in a low lying area, get to higher ground immediately.
- If told to evacuate, do so immediately.
chunks.heading: Stay informed and move to safety

chunks.title: Flood Safety — Actions During Heavy Rain and Flooding
chunks.content:
- Turn Around, Don't Drown. Do not drive into flooded roadways or around barricades.
- 12 inches of water can float a car or small SUV; 18 inches can carry away large vehicles.
- A vehicle caught in swiftly moving water can be swept away in seconds.
chunks.heading: Driving

chunks.title: Flood Safety — Actions During Heavy Rain and Flooding
chunks.content:
- Do not walk through flood waters. Six inches of moving water can knock you off your feet.
- If trapped by moving water, move to the highest possible point and call emergency services if possible.
chunks.heading: On foot

chunks.title: Flood Safety — Actions During Heavy Rain and Flooding
chunks.content:
- Avoid basements or rooms where water covers electrical outlets or cords are submerged.
- Leave immediately if you see sparks or hear buzzing, crackling, snapping or popping noises.
- Stay out of water that may have electricity in it.
chunks.heading: Electrical hazards

chunks.title: Air Quality Index Basics
chunks.content:
Source: AirNow (US EPA and partners), "AQI Basics".
Retrieved 2026-08-05. US federal government work, public domain.
chunks.heading: Air Quality Index — Categories and Health Meaning

chunks.title: Air Quality Index Basics
chunks.content:
- AQI 0 to 50, Good: air quality is satisfactory, and air pollution poses little or no risk.
- AQI 51 to 100, Moderate: air quality is acceptable. There may be a risk for some people, particularly those who are unusually sensitive to air pollution.
- AQI 101 to 150, Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups: members of sensitive groups may experience health effects. The general public is less likely to be affected.
- AQI 151 to 200, Unhealthy: some members of the general public may experience health effects; members of sensitive groups may experience more serious health effects.
- AQI 201 to 300, Very Unhealthy: health alert. The risk of health effects is increased for everyone.
- AQI 301 and above, Hazardous: health warning of emergency conditions. Everyone is more likely to be affected.
chunks.heading: Categories

chunks.title: Air Quality Index Basics
chunks.content:
- The higher the AQI value, the greater the level of pollution and the greater the health concern.
- Values at or below 100 are generally considered satisfactory.
- Values above 100 indicate increasingly unhealthy conditions, first for sensitive groups and then for everyone.
chunks.heading: Interpreting the value
